title: Croup — Westley Score & Management
keywords: barky cough seal-like stridor hoarse voice
dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg single dose max 12 mg all severities
observe at least 2-3 hours after epinephrine before discharge, effect wanes by ~2h
sources: Westley CR, et al. Nebulized racemic epinephrine by IPPB for the treatment of croup: a double-blind study. Am J Dis Child. 1978;132(5):484-487 (original scoring system).
Croup: Rapid Evidence Review. Am Fam Physician. 2026 (dosing equivalence data, epinephrine time course, discharge criteria).
Bjornson C, Russell K. Nebulized epinephrine for croup in children. Cochrane Database Syst Rev (foundational epinephrine evidence base).

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap. Westley score table and severity-tiered management verified against the 2026 AFP rapid evidence review; included the less commonly known finding that low-dose dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg) performs comparably to the standard 0.6 mg/kg for most patients, since that's a real stewardship-relevant nuance rather than boilerplate.

ageRange: Typically 6 months - 3 years, peak ~2 years; can occur up to age 6
purpose: Score croup severity with the Westley score and match treatment (dexamethasone alone vs. + nebulized epinephrine) to that severity — with the discharge-timing question after epinephrine that trips people up most.

body.text: Barky/seal-like cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor from viral (usually parainfluenza) upper-airway inflammation. Symptoms are classically worse at night and with agitation/crying — assess the child as calm as possible, since agitation itself worsens the exam findings and can overestimate severity.

items: Mild (< 2): single dose of oral dexamethasone plus supportive care and reassurance (cool air/mist has no proven benefit but is low-risk and often used); discharge home if the child otherwise looks well.

Moderate-severe (≥ 3): dexamethasone PLUS nebulized epinephrine. Epinephrine improves signs of respiratory distress within 10-30 minutes, with effect sustained for roughly an hour and largely gone by about 2 hours — this decay curve is exactly why observation after dosing matters (see below).

Impending respiratory failure (≥ 12): treat as above but with immediate escalation — prepare for advanced airway management, involve anesthesia/ENT/PICU early, and do not delay epinephrine while arranging disposition.

body.text: Standard dose: 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg), single dose, PO/IM/IV — all equally effective, oral is preferred when tolerated. A genuinely useful nuance: 0.15 mg/kg and 0.3 mg/kg doses have shown comparable clinical effectiveness to 0.6 mg/kg in mild-to-moderate croup in multiple studies, though 0.6 mg/kg remains the most commonly used and the safe default when dosing precision or follow-up is uncertain.
Discharge after nebulized epinephrine — the part that gets missed

Epinephrine's effect wanes within roughly 2 hours, so a child who looks great at 20 minutes post-dose is NOT ready for discharge on that basis alone. Observe for at least 2-3 hours after the last epinephrine dose, watching for rebound symptoms as the effect wears off, before discharging. A child needing a second epinephrine dose, or one who rebounds significantly, warrants a longer observation period or admission.

items: Discharge criteria: sustained improvement through the observation window, no stridor at rest, adequate oral intake, and reliable caregivers who understand return precautions.

Admission: impending respiratory failure, multiple epinephrine doses needed, significant rebound after observation, or an atypical/prolonged course raising concern for bacterial tracheitis or another diagnosis.

buildNote: kind: reference with an embedded severity table rather than an embedded calculator — the Westley score is a clean additive point score and could become a calculator later, but the discharge-timing pitfall (epinephrine wearing off before disposition) is the higher-yield teaching point and is prose/callout content, not a number. Pairs with bronchiolitis-management and peds-rsi-decision-card (impending-failure escalation); peds-tool has no related[] field, so cross-link noted here in prose.
